name: Airbus in Botswana — market entry strategy
description: Team school project (NEOMA, Live Business Transition Case): an entry strategy for Airbus in Botswana, from the choice of segment to the joint-venture structure, roadmap, investment, ESG plan and risks.
context: The brief, in a course built as a “live business transition case”: in teams of four, evaluate the strategic internationalisation of Airbus into a foreign market chosen from an approved list, assess the host country's business environment and its strategic fit with Airbus, and deliver a coherent market entry plan. The project mirrors a real corporate transition project and had to apply international business frameworks (PESTEL, CAGE, SWOT, VRIO, industry analysis, entry-mode theory, CSR).

Our team chose Botswana. After a mid-term presentation on the country, the final deliverable was a 20-minute presentation followed by questions, with a written learning document. It is a group project: the result is a team effort, not mine alone.

work.title: The strategic pivot
work.text: From selling aircraft to anchoring a local ecosystem.
points: Shift from a market-seeking to an efficiency-seeking approach, based on Botswana's institutional strengths (property rights, judicial effectiveness, fiscal health, educated workforce).
Competitors were turning sales into lock-in through local after-sales; Airbus had the capabilities at group level but no local presence.

work.title: Target segment
work.text: Helicopter maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) and completion (customisation): recurring revenue and high-skill services that fit a country with limited heavy industry but a well-educated workforce.

work.title: Entry mode and governance
work.text: A strategic joint venture with the Botswana Development Corporation and the civil aviation authority.
points: 51% Airbus / 49% partner: local legitimacy and fast-tracked permits, without the IP risk of licensing or the 'foreign extraction' image of a wholly owned subsidiary.
Airbus keeps a technical veto on safety, maintenance standards and IP.

work.title: Location and roadmap 2026–2028
work.text: A hub in the special economic zone at Gaborone airport, built in three phases.
points: 2026: land, facility construction, EASA and local certifications, logistics corridor from the port of Durban.
2027: MRO launch timed with the AviaDev Africa event; regional maintenance contracts.
2028: completion centre for medical, VIP or government helicopter configurations.
Applied R&D with a local university on 'hot, high and dusty' operating conditions.

work.title: Investment, ESG and risks
work.text: A business case with its conditions of success.
points: $30–35M capex, 40+ local engineers and technicians trained to EASA standards, break-even in year 5.
ESG plan: solar power for part of the hangar's energy, sustainable aviation fuel for test flights, anti-corruption and audit transparency.
Risk matrix (supply chain, currency, skills) with a mitigation for each, and a clear list of what Airbus should not do.

transcript.title: Synthesis of mid-term insights
text: Use AviaDev 2026 (Gaborone, June) to sign and announce the partnership with the Civil Aviation Authority of Botswana (50+ countries and 48+ airlines).
Legal shield: best intellectual-property protection in the region (Property Rights 74.1, Judicial Effectiveness 70.5). Safest option in the region for a capital-intensive manufacturing facility.
Strong scores in Fiscal Health (90.4) and Trade Freedom (78.8), low inflation of 2.82%, and an educated workforce (79% advanced education).
The strategic pivot: Airbus is shifting from a market-seeking approach to an efficiency-seeking one.

transcript.title: Internal & competitive assessment
text: Existing footprint : Airbus already operates in Botswana through defence contracts (H125 Police / Super Puma Army) :
Established institutional relationship while competitors must build from scratch

Capability gap to close : Embraer (sold 3 jets to Air Botswana) and Leonardo are converting sales into lock-in via local aftersales. Airbus has the MRO (Maintenance, Repair, Overhaul) and training capabilities at group level to counter this, but has no local deployment yet.
The competitive lever : A local technical footprint at SSKIA transforms Airbus from distant supplier to ecosystem anchor.
For clients, switching costs is structural rather than contractual.
The strategic implication : Airbus's A220-300 product advantage only becomes durable if backed by a local service presence, which justifies the entry mode choice...

transcript.title: Targeted segment: why helicopters & MRO?
text: The Choice: Segment focus on MRO (Maintenance, Repair, Overhaul) and Completion (Customization)
Evidence: Highest recurring revenue logic. It fits the local manufacturing limitations (5.55% of GDP) by focusing on high-skill services (79% advanced education).

transcript.title: Recommended entry strategy: strategic joint venture
text: Mode: Joint Venture (JV) with the Botswana Development Corporation (BDC) and CAAB.

Why? Botswana's Investment Freedom is moderate (50.0). Partnering with the BDC grants Airbus "National Project Status", which fast-tracks work permits and land acquisition within the Special Economic Zone.
A 100% subsidiary would be seen as foreign extraction, while a simple licensing agreement would risk our IP.
A JV offers the right balance of local legitimacy and corporate control.

transcript.title: Partnership architecture & governance
text: Equity & responsibility split: Airbus (51%) / BDC (49%).
Airbus role: technology transfer, global supply-chain integration and EASA certification.
BDC role: local infrastructure management, labour relations and government liaison.
Technical veto: Airbus keeps 100% veto power over safety protocols, maintenance standards and IP-related decisions.
Judicial safeguard: contractual enforcement is backed by Botswana's high Judicial Efficiency score (70.5).

transcript.title: Location & innovation network
text: Local supply & maintenance cluster: integration of regional SMEs for non-critical component supply, reducing lead times and building ecosystem resilience.

Strategic SEZ hub (Gaborone): direct runway access at Sir Seretse Khama International Airport for flight testing and client handovers; SEZ benefits include corporate tax exemptions, streamlined customs and zero import duties on critical aviation parts.

Applied R&D partnership (BIUST University): engineering adaptations for "hot, high and dusty" African operating environments, with a continuous feedback loop between local academia and Airbus engineers to improve fleet reliability.

transcript.title: Implementation roadmap (2026–2028)
text: Phase 1 — Foundation & certification (2026): secure SEZ land allocation and start building a climate-controlled facility; obtain dual EASA (Europe) and CAAB (Botswana) site certifications; establish a secure Durban–Gaborone logistics corridor.
Phase 2 — Operations & commercial launch (2027): inaugurate the MRO facility alongside AviaDev Africa; start regional maintenance contracts targeting fleets across the 16 SADC countries.

Phase 3 — Expansion to a completion centre (2028): move from maintenance to final assembly with a Regional Completion Center for local customisation of Airbus helicopter kits (medical, VIP or military configurations).

transcript.title: Required capabilities & investment
text: Financial commitment ($30M–$35M CAPEX): hangar construction, specialised diagnostic tooling, spare-parts inventory and advanced MRO equipment.

Human capital & knowledge transfer: an Airbus training programme with European experts forming a core local team; target of 40+ local engineers and technicians certified to EASA standards within three years.
Logistics & supply-chain security: fast-track route from Durban port to the SEZ, and 3-month buffer stocks of critical avionics to avoid AOG (Aircraft On Ground) delays.

transcript.title: Sustainability criteria (ESG)
text: Environmental — Solar-powered infrastructure: Botswana's 320+ sunny days a year could cover 30% of the hangar's energy needs; phased use of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) for engine tests and maintenance flights, in line with Airbus's Net Zero 2050 roadmap.

Social — Knowledge transfer with BIUST University to certify 50+ local technicians to EASA standards within three years; maintenance support for anti-poaching and wildlife-monitoring fleets (e.g. Okavango Delta surveillance).

Governance — Airbus's global anti-corruption standards applied within the JV (Botswana is the least corrupt country in the region, Government Integrity 60.1); joint oversight with the BDC and quarterly public reporting against IFRS standards.

transcript.title: Risk prioritisation
text: Risks ranked on a probability × impact matrix.

head: Risk
Probability / impact
Mitigation
rows: 3-month buffer stock of critical avionics in the SEZ
Contracts denominated in USD for regional clients
Partnership with BIUST for a steady talent pipeline

transcript.title: What Airbus should not do
text: No heavy manufacturing: do not build fuselages or wings (no local heavy industry).
No operations outside the SEZ: higher taxes and red tape would kill the business case.
No early diversification: focus strictly on helicopters and MRO for the first five years.

transcript.title: Business case & actionable recommendations
text: Returns: break-even in year 5; strategic return through a lock-in effect that supports future A220 sales.
Immediate actions: sign the agreement with the Botswana Development Corporation and secure a land plot at SSKIA.
Success factor: make Gaborone the technical face of Airbus in Africa.

transcript.title: Thank you
text: Thank you. Any questions?

name: Devinci — Asia-Pacific expansion strategy
description: Team school project on a business case: which Asia-Pacific markets a Canadian mountain bike maker should prioritise, and how to enter them.
context: A case study on Devinci, a Canadian bike manufacturer that wanted to reach 1,000 mountain bike sales a year in the Asia-Pacific region within three years. Our team of five had to decide which markets to prioritise and which entry modes would limit risk while supporting growth. The result is a team effort, not mine alone.

The original case, written by HEC Montréal and licensed to the school for teaching, is protected by copyright, so it cannot be published here. This page only presents our team's own analysis and recommendations.

work.title: Method
work.text: From the company's track record to a market-by-market comparison.
points: Review of the brand's past international expansion and a SWOT analysis.
Comparison of Japan, Australia, New Zealand and China on market potential, import tariffs, ease of doing business, riding infrastructure and cultural distance.
Assessment of the brand's competitive strengths in each market, then a prioritisation matrix (attractiveness × competitive strength).

work.title: Recommendation
work.text: Two priority markets, each with its own entry mode.
points: Japan and Australia as priorities; New Zealand as a selective niche; China as a secondary, later option given its regulatory complexity and cultural distance.
Japan: joint venture, to navigate relationship-based distribution and reach ski resorts, the hubs for downhill riding.
Australia: direct exporting, thanks to low entry barriers, a shared language and a very large trail network.

transcript.title: Context and decision to be made
text: Context: founded in 1987 in Quebec, Devinci is a bike manufacturer known for high-performance aluminium frames and strong R&D. By 2018 it had expanded into the U.S. and Europe, with exports at 55% of sales in 2016.
A new corporate objective targets 20% annual growth, and the threat of U.S. tariffs makes diversification essential.

Decision: Global Brand Manager Simon Brodeur must propose a strategy to reach 1,000 mountain-bike sales a year in the APAC region within three years — which markets to prioritise and which entry modes best limit risk while ensuring growth.

transcript.title: Evaluation of Devinci's international efforts to date
text: Performance: Exports grew from 5% (2010) to 55% (2016) of total sales.
Approach: Glocal strategy, centralized R&D and high-end manufacturing in Canada with local logistics support.
Choice of Regions: Initial expansion focused on culturally similar or high-demand
Western markets (U.S. and Europe).
While the first U.S. attempt failed in 2006, the second expansion in 2011 was successful due to better risk management and a focus on high-end mountain bikes.

transcript.title: SWOT analysis
text: Strengths: Patent (Split Pivot); reputation; brand identity (Steve Smith)
Weaknesses: Low brand awareness; export costs
Opportunities: China: latent demand of US$2.2 billion; Japan: 543 ski resorts; Australia / New Zealand: 14,117 km / 9,447 km of trails
Threats: Import taxes in some countries (China 13%); cultural complexity (partnerships); strong established competitors (Giant, Merida)

transcript.title: Universal competitive advantages
text: Technological expertise: all high-end models use the patented Split Pivot suspension, a clear advantage over mass-market competitors.
R&D excellence: a 15-person R&D department, including five full-time engineers.
"Made in Canada" prestige: as the last mass producer of bikes in Canada, Devinci leverages a boutique image and aluminium-welding craftsmanship.
Racing credibility: the Devinci Global Racing team provides technical feedback and builds awareness among enthusiasts.

head: Market
Devinci's specific competitive strengths
rows: Shock-resistant aluminium frames suited to 14,117 km of trails; Individualism score of 90 matches the "Ride Canadian" lifestyle branding.
High-end enthusiast niche with low psychic distance (Individualism 79, ease of business rank 1); New Zealand athletes on the 2018 racing team give local legitimacy to the Spartan and Wilson models.
Downhill focus (Wilson) matches 543 ski resorts used as gravity-riding hubs; 0% tariff protects margins or funds local promotion.
In a market dominated by low-cost bikes, Devinci's boutique status and high-end carbon assembly signal quality to premium clients.

transcript.title: Market to prioritise: matrix
text: Prioritisation matrix crossing market attractiveness and competitive strength: Japan and Australia in zone A, New Zealand in zone A/B, China in zone B/C.

transcript.title: Recommended modes of entry
text: Japan — joint venture: a local partner navigates the high Power Distance (54) and relationship-based distribution; a JV helps target the 543 ski resorts for the Wilson downhill line; costs and management effort are shared while the 0% tariff keeps prices competitive.

Australia — direct exporting: low entry barriers and high cultural similarity to Canada; ease of business (rank 14) and a shared language make direct retailer relationships easy; 14,117 km of trails offer a volume market.
